scope: Core PostgreSQL querying and relational database design; no learner records

concepts.description: Project columns and computed expressions from a table with SELECT, control duplicate rows and assign readable output column names.
learning_objectives: Project the required columns and expressions in a SELECT list.
Assign readable output names with column aliases.
Remove duplicate result rows with DISTINCT and state the cost of doing so.
Predict the result columns produced by SELECT * and by an explicit column list.

concepts.description: Filter source rows with a boolean WHERE predicate that combines comparison, range, membership and NULL-aware conditions.
learning_objectives: Build a WHERE predicate that keeps exactly the rows required by a specification.
Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT while respecting operator precedence.
Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL instead of equality when NULL values are involved.
Explain why a predicate that compares with NULL yields unknown rather than true.

concepts.description: Combine rows from related tables with JOIN, writing correct ON predicates and selecting the join type that matches the required result.
learning_objectives: Translate a relationship between tables into a correct JOIN ... ON condition.
Choose an inner or outer join based on whether unmatched rows must be kept.
Diagnose unexpected duplicate rows caused by a one-to-many join key.
Join three or more tables without losing the intended row population.

concepts.description: Group rows into sets with GROUP BY and compute per-group aggregates such as counts, sums and averages.
learning_objectives: Group rows by one or more columns to produce one output row per group.
Apply aggregate functions to summarize each group.
Distinguish a grouping column from an aggregated expression in the SELECT list.
Explain how a NULL grouping key forms its own group.

concepts.description: Filter grouped results with HAVING, distinguishing group-level predicates from row-level WHERE conditions.
learning_objectives: Apply HAVING to keep only groups that satisfy an aggregate condition.
Choose WHERE for row filtering and HAVING for group filtering inside the same query.
Explain why a WHERE clause cannot reference an aggregate result directly.
Predict the difference in output when a predicate moves from WHERE to HAVING.

concepts.description: Compose queries with scalar, row, IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries in the SELECT, FROM and WHERE clauses.
learning_objectives: Use a scalar subquery where a single computed value is required.
Compare IN, EXISTS and join formulations for the same filtering task.
Write a correlated subquery that references the current outer row.
Explain when a subquery in FROM acts as an independent derived table.

concepts.description: Model a problem domain as entities, attributes and relationships, then translate the model into a relational schema with keys.
learning_objectives: Identify entities, attributes and relationships from a written domain description.
Determine cardinality and participation constraints for each relationship.
Convert an ER model into tables with primary and foreign keys.
Detect modeling choices that would duplicate data or lose required relationships.

concepts.description: Evaluate relational schemas with functional dependencies and normal forms, and decompose them to reduce redundancy and update anomalies.
learning_objectives: Explain which update, insert and delete anomalies normalization is intended to prevent.
Derive candidate keys from a set of functional dependencies.
Decompose a relation into higher normal forms while preserving its dependencies.
Verify that a decomposition is lossless and does not fabricate rows.

concepts.description: Reason about functional dependencies, attribute closure and candidate keys as the theoretical basis for relational design.
learning_objectives: Determine whether a functional dependency is implied by a given set of dependencies.
Compute the attribute closure of a determinant.
Derive all candidate keys of a relation from its functional dependencies.
Use inference rules to simplify a dependency set without changing its closure.

concepts.description: Apply first normal form by keeping every attribute atomic and eliminating repeating groups from relational tables.
learning_objectives: Identify repeating groups and multivalued cells that violate first normal form.
Restructure a non-atomic table into rows whose attribute values are atomic.
Explain why storing lists in a single column complicates querying and constraints.
Distinguish the requirements of first normal form from those of higher normal forms.

concepts.description: Apply second normal form by removing partial dependencies of non-key attributes on part of a composite candidate key.
learning_objectives: Detect a partial dependency on part of a composite candidate key.
Decompose a relation in first normal form into second normal form.
Explain why second normal form is automatic when the key is a single attribute.
Verify that the resulting decomposition preserves the original information.

concepts.description: Apply third normal form by eliminating transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on other non-key attributes.
learning_objectives: Detect transitive dependencies among non-key attributes.
Decompose a second-normal-form relation into third normal form.
Compare third normal form with Boyce-Codd normal form for a given schema.
Explain the redundancy that a transitive dependency introduces.

concepts.description: Retrieve rows and columns from a single table with SELECT, choosing projected values, filtering rows with WHERE and controlling presentation order.
learning_objectives: Identify the clauses that form a basic SELECT statement and the logical order in which they are evaluated.
Choose the columns and expressions needed to produce a requested result set.
Filter source rows with a WHERE predicate and explain how NULL affects the comparison.
Order result rows explicitly whenever the presentation order matters.

concepts.description: Combine rows from two or more related relations with join predicates, distinguishing inner from outer joins and controlling row multiplication.
learning_objectives: Write an inner join that combines rows from two tables on a matching key.
Compare inner, left, right and full outer joins when unmatched rows must be preserved.
Explain how a missing or non-unique join key changes the number of returned rows.
Choose explicit JOIN ... ON syntax over implicit comma joins in new queries.

concepts.description: Use database indexes to accelerate selective lookups and joins while accounting for their write, storage and maintenance costs.
learning_objectives: Explain how an index avoids a sequential scan for a selective predicate.
Decide which columns and column order belong in a composite index for a query workload.
Compare the read benefit of an index with its write and storage overhead.
Verify index use through EXPLAIN instead of assuming the planner will choose it.

clos.title: Construct and reason about PostgreSQL queries
Model relational data and normalize schemas

questions.prompt: Which clause filters rows in a SELECT statement?
Which join returns only matching rows from both tables?
Write a query that returns all customer names from the customers table.

datasets.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id int, name text); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Alice');
CREATE TABLE customers (id int, name text);

questions.prompt: Explain why indexes speed up reads but slow down writes.

rubrics.criteria: Mentions lookup benefit OR write cost
Covers B-tree lookup cost and write amplification

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table is read frequently by a filtered column and also receives frequent INSERT and UPDATE operations. Explain how adding a B-tree index affects both workloads, and when that index may not be worthwhile.

rubrics.criteria: Does not identify a relevant effect of the index on either the filtered reads or the writes
Correctly identifies either faster filtered reads or added INSERT and UPDATE work, but does not explain the other workload
Explains both faster filtered reads and index maintenance on writes, but gives an incomplete reason for when the index may not be worthwhile
Explains selective B-tree lookups, maintenance cost on INSERT and UPDATE, and a justified case where low selectivity or write-heavy use does not merit the index

questions.prompt: Which SELECT clause chooses the returned attributes?
Which condition excludes a row whose amount is NULL?

options.option_text: amount IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL

questions.prompt: What does an INNER JOIN return when a row has no matching key?

options.option_text: It always produces a NULL-extended row

questions.prompt: What does GROUP BY region_id establish for SUM(amount)?

options.option_text: A sort order for individual sales
A unique primary key on the table

questions.prompt: When is HAVING evaluated relative to grouping?

options.option_text: After groups and aggregates are formed

questions.prompt: What happens when a scalar aggregate subquery computes AVG on no non-NULL values?
How is a many-to-many relationship mapped to relational tables?

options.option_text: Use a junction table referencing both entity keys
Place a comma-separated key list in one column
Merge every entity into a single row

questions.prompt: Which change addresses a repeating multivalued attribute?

options.option_text: Store the values as a longer delimited string
Move its values into a related relation with atomic attributes

questions.prompt: What does the dependency student_id -> email mean?

options.option_text: Each student_id determines at most one email value
Each email must determine a student_id

questions.prompt: Which representation satisfies atomic attribute values?

options.option_text: One enrollment record per student and course
A course column containing a list of course IDs

questions.prompt: Which dependency violates 2NF for a non-prime attribute with composite key (student_id, course_id)?
Which decomposition addresses student_id -> dept_id -> dept_name?

options.option_text: Replace dept_id with a comma-separated list
Keep department names in a department relation keyed by dept_id
Add dept_name to every composite key

questions.prompt: Return the id and amount of every sale.

datasets.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North'),(2,'South'),(3,'West'); INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,1,10.00),(2,1,20.00),(3,2,30.00),(4,2,NULL);
CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North');

questions.prompt: Return IDs of sales with an amount of at least 20.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT id FROM sales WHERE amount >= 20

datasets.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North'),(2,'South'),(3,'West'); INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,1,10.00),(2,1,20.00),(3,2,30.00),(4,2,NULL);
CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North');

questions.prompt: Return each sale ID and its matching region label using a JOIN.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT s.id, r.label FROM sales s JOIN regions r ON r.id=s.region_id

datasets.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North'),(2,'South'),(3,'West'); INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,1,10.00),(2,1,20.00),(3,2,30.00),(4,2,NULL);
CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North');

questions.prompt: Return each region_id and the total non-NULL sale amount using GROUP BY.
questions.reference_answer: SELECT region_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region_id

datasets.setup_sql: CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North'),(2,'South'),(3,'West'); INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,1,10.00),(2,1,20.00),(3,2,30.00),(4,2,NULL);
CREATE TABLE regions(id INT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE sales(id INT PRIMARY KEY, region_id INT, amount NUMERIC(8,2)); INSERT INTO regions VALUES (1,'North');

questions.reference_answer: SELECT region_id FROM sales GROUP BY region_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 30

questions.prompt: For Enrollment(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, dept_id, dept_name, grade), assume (student_id, course_id) is the key and student_id -> student_name, course_id -> course_title, student_id -> dept_id, dept_id -> dept_name. Explain the ER relationships, functional dependencies and a decomposition from 1NF through 2NF to 3NF. Justify lossless joins and dependency preservation.
questions.reference_answer: Separate Student(student_id, student_name, dept_id), Department(dept_id, dept_name), Course(course_id, course_title), and Enrollment(student_id, course_id, grade). Identify partial dependencies on student_id and course_id and the transitive department dependency. Enrollment represents the many-to-many association. Key-based joins reconstruct enrollment facts without spurious tuples and each specified dependency is enforced in a relation.

rubrics.criteria: No coherent dependency analysis or valid decomposition
Identifies at least one relevant dependency but decomposition is incomplete
Provides correct dependency analysis and decomposition with a minor omission in justification
Identifies keys and dependencies, reaches the stated normal form, and justifies lossless join and dependency preservation
